what_it_means: Money that has arrived but has not yet been given a job. The single most prominent number in the app.
where_it_appears: Budget header. Also a docs page title.
translator_note: Alternatives: 'Verfügbar zum Zuweisen' (precise but long), 'Nicht zugewiesen'. Chose the short idiomatic one because this sits in a header. HIGH PRIORITY REVIEW — this is the flagship term.

what_it_means: To give money a job by moving it into a category.
where_it_appears: Primary action verb throughout the budget screen.
translator_note: Must stay consistent with ready_to_assign choice.

what_it_means: Budget grid column: how much money was put into this category this month.
where_it_appears: Budget table column header. One of the core three (Assigned / Activity / Available).

what_it_means: Budget grid column: money that moved in or out of this category this month.
translator_note: 'Umsatz' is the German banking term for turnover and may read more naturally to a finance audience. Reviewer decision.

what_it_means: Budget grid column: what is actually left to spend in this category right now.
where_it_appears: Budget table column header. The number users check most.

what_it_means: An envelope that holds money for a purpose (Groceries, Rent).
translator_note: Plural: Kategorien

what_it_means: A collapsible heading that groups related categories.
where_it_appears: Budget screen structure. Docs page title.
translator_note: Confirm 'Kategoriengruppe' vs 'Kategoriegruppe' — both appear in German usage.

what_it_means: The plan for a month, and also the top-level container users can have several of.
translator_note: 'Haushaltsplan' is more native but 'Budget' is widely understood and shorter. Note the German market term for this app category is 'Haushaltsbuch' — relevant for marketing copy, probably not for in-app labels.

what_it_means: The method: every unit of currency gets a job until nothing is unassigned.
translator_note: German finance media uses the English term (observed as 'Zero-Based-Budget-Ansatz'). 'Nullbasiertes Budgetieren' exists but reads academic.

what_it_means: The cash-in-envelopes metaphor Budgero digitizes.
where_it_appears: Marketing and docs. High SEO value in German.
translator_note: VERIFIED as the established German term via market research — has its own content ecosystem and search demand. Highest-confidence entry in this file. Adjacent trend term: 'Cashstuffing'.

what_it_means: A category whose Available has gone negative.
translator_note: 'Überschritten' (exceeded) is the alternative. 'Überzogen' carries the overdrawn connotation which fits better.

what_it_means: A real-world place money sits (checking, savings, credit card).
where_it_appears: Sidebar, docs page title. NOTE: distinct from a user login account — check context before translating.
translator_note: Login account is 'Benutzerkonto' — keep distinct.

what_it_means: An account whose balance feeds Ready to Assign.
An account tracked for net worth but excluded from budgeting.
where_it_appears: Account settings. Inbound transfers from these credit Ready to Assign.
translator_note: Long. If it appears in a badge, consider 'Extern' or 'Nicht im Budget'.

what_it_means: A single movement of money.
translator_note: 'Buchung' or 'Umsatz' are the native banking terms and may read better to German users. Reviewer decision — this term appears constantly.

what_it_means: Who money went to, or came from.
where_it_appears: Transaction table column, transaction form field.
translator_note: 'Zahlungsempfänger' is precise but 19 chars vs 5 — will break the table column. 'Empfänger' matches German online banking. Note it reads oddly for inflows; consider whether a neutral term works better.

what_it_means: Money coming in.
translator_note: 'Zufluss' is more literal; 'Einnahme' is the everyday term.

what_it_means: Money going out.
A transaction confirmed against the real account.
translator_note: 'Gebucht' is the German banking term for posted. 'Bestätigt' is the generic alternative.

what_it_means: A transaction entered but not yet confirmed against the real account.
translator_note: Must mirror the 'cleared' choice.

what_it_means: To confirm the app balance matches the real account balance.
translator_note: Noun form: 'Kontenabgleich'.

what_it_means: Movement of money between two of the user's own accounts.
translator_note: 'Überweisung' means a bank transfer to a third party — wrong sense here. 'Umbuchung' is the internal-move sense. Worth a careful review.

what_it_means: One transaction divided across multiple categories.
A funding plan attached to a category. Four types across spending and savings flavors.
where_it_appears: Docs page title, category detail. NOTE: distinct from 'target' — a goal HAS a target.
translator_note: Must stay distinct from target_amount / target_date below.

what_it_means: The number a goal is aiming at. A parameter OF a goal, not a synonym for goal.
The date a savings goal should be reached by.
What a goal requires to stay on track this month.
An automation that acts on matching transactions.
The subsystem that evaluates and applies rules.
translator_note: 'Regel-Engine' is the anglicized alternative and common in German software UIs.

what_it_means: A transaction scheduled to repeat.
translator_note: Do NOT use 'Dauerauftrag' — that specifically means a bank standing order.

what_it_means: Total assets minus total liabilities.
Following loan and credit-card balances down to zero.
translator_note: Long compound. 'Schuldenübersicht' (debt overview) may read better.

what_it_means: A container holding budgets, shareable with other users.
The password that derives the encryption key. Cannot be recovered — distinct from the login password.
where_it_appears: Docs page title, onboarding, security settings.
translator_note: Keep clearly distinct from 'Anmeldepasswort' (login password) — users conflating these is a support burden.

what_it_means: The server cannot read user data. Core product claim.
where_it_appears: Marketing, security docs. High value in the German market.
translator_note: Keep English — it's the established technical term in German security writing. Pair with a plain-language gloss on first use.

what_it_means: Data encrypted on device, never readable server-side.
translator_note: Established German term, widely understood. Strong marketing keyword for the DE privacy segment.

what_it_means: Running Budgero on your own infrastructure.
translator_note: The English 'Self-Hosting' is also common in German technical writing and may be better for SEO.

what_it_means: Full functionality without a network connection.
Bringing transactions in from a CSV file.
A saved analytical view over transactions.
A what-if projection over the budget.
A tracked product warranty with an expiry.
translator_note: German distinguishes 'Garantie' (voluntary manufacturer warranty) from 'Gewährleistung' (statutory). Confirm which the feature actually tracks — this is a legally loaded distinction in DE.

what_it_means: Giving another user access to a budget.
Support for accounts and budgets in different currencies.
where_it_appears: Docs page title, marketing. Key differentiator for the EU market.
translator_note: 'Mehrwährungsfähig' is the more native adjective. Reviewer decision.
